content: Beta-glucans, also known as β-glucans, are polysaccharides found in the bran of cereal grains, the cell walls of baker's yeast, certain fungi, and various mushrooms. Among cereal-based beta-glucans, barley and oats are the richest sources, with smaller amounts found in rye and wheat. These compounds are valuable in human nutrition as soluble fiber supplements and texturing agents. However, in brewing, excessive beta-glucans can increase wort viscosity, causing complications. Beta-glucans derived from baker's yeast exhibit structural differences between their soluble (1,3/1,4) and insoluble (1,3/1,6) forms. The insoluble form, due to its branched structure, demonstrates greater biological activity. Yeast-derived beta-glucans are particularly noted for their immunomodulatory properties. The structural differences between soluble and insoluble beta-glucans significantly influence their applications, mechanisms of action, and overall biological activity. Glucans are polysaccharides composed solely of glucose molecules. Beta-1,3-D-glucans consist of chains of D-glucose molecules linked at the 1 and 3 positions. The most biologically active forms of beta-1,3-D-glucans are those with 1,6 side chains branching off the main 1,3 backbone, referred to as beta-1,3/1,6-glucans. Research suggests that the immune activity of beta-glucans is determined more by the frequency, location, and length of these side chains than by the backbone itself. Additionally, some beta-glucans exist as single-stranded chains, while others form double or triple-stranded helical chains. In some cases, proteins linked to the beta-1,3-glucan backbone may contribute to therapeutic activity. Beta-glucans have shown potential in enhancing immune system function, but research in this area is still in its early stages. There is ongoing debate regarding the molecular weight, structure, and source of beta-1,3-glucans that provide the greatest therapeutic benefits. One of the most common sources of beta-1,3-D-glucans is the cell wall of baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). Beta-glucans are also extracted from the bran of grains like oats and barley, as well as from certain types of seaweed and mushrooms such as Reishi, Shiitake, and Maitake. Yeast-derived beta-glucans are often insoluble, whereas grain-derived beta-glucans tend to be soluble. Beta-1,3-D-glucans are classified as biological response modifiers due to their ability to activate the immune system. Unlike agents that overstimulate the immune system, which can be harmful in individuals with autoimmune diseases, allergies, or yeast infections, beta-glucans enhance immune function without causing overactivation. They achieve this by activating phagocytes, immune cells that trap and destroy foreign substances like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. Beta-glucans also reportedly lower elevated LDL cholesterol levels, aid in wound healing, prevent infections, enhance natural killer (NK) cell function, and assist in cancer prevention and treatment. Clinical Applications Cancer Beta-glucans have been used as immunoadjuvant therapy for cancer since the 1980s, particularly in Japan. Studies have demonstrated their anti-tumor and anti-cancer properties. For example, intralesional administration of beta-1,3-glucans has led to rapid tumor shrinkage. In mice, beta-glucans combined with interferon-gamma inhibited tumor establishment and liver metastasis. Beta-glucans have also been shown to enhance the effects of chemotherapy. In bladder cancer studies, combining cyclophosphamide with yeast-derived beta-glucans reduced mortality in mice. In human patients with advanced gastric or colorectal cancer, beta-glucans derived from Shiitake mushrooms, when used alongside chemotherapy, prolonged survival times compared to chemotherapy alone. Preclinical studies have shown that a soluble yeast beta-glucan product, Imprime PGG, significantly improves long-term survival when combined with monoclonal antibodies or cancer vaccines. This effect is not due to enhanced antibody-specific killing but rather a unique mechanism involving neutrophils primed with beta-glucans. These neutrophils, typically not involved in cancer destruction, are activated to target tumors when beta-glucans are used in conjunction with complement-activating monoclonal antibodies. This mechanism has been effective against various cancers in combination with specific monoclonal antibodies. Prevention of Infection Numerous studies and clinical trials have evaluated the role of beta-glucans in reducing post-surgical infections and treating anthrax infections. For example, in high-risk surgical patients, beta-glucan therapy reduced serious post-operative infections by 39%. Beta-glucans have also been shown to enhance phagocytic activity, improving the immune system's response to bacterial challenges. In animal studies, orally administered beta-glucans protected mice against anthrax infections, with survival rates significantly higher than in control groups. Radiation Exposure Beta-glucans have demonstrated radioprotective properties, reversing myelosuppression caused by chemotherapeutic drugs and enhancing hematopoiesis. In mice exposed to lethal doses of radiation, beta-glucans improved survival rates. These findings suggest potential applications for beta-glucans in chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and nuclear emergencies. Septic Shock Beta-glucans enhance the immune system's ability to combat septic infections by priming leukocytes to locate and kill bacteria more effectively. Studies have shown that beta-glucans reduce septic shock by killing bacteria in the bloodstream and protecting against oxidative organ injury. Surgery and Wound Healing Beta-glucans have been shown to improve wound healing by enhancing macrophage function, reducing infections, and increasing the tensile strength of scar tissue. In post-splenectomy models, beta-glucans significantly improved survival rates. These findings suggest that beta-glucans may be a valuable adjunct to standard surgical care. Allergic Rhinitis Orally administered beta-glucans have been shown to reduce cytokines like IL-4 and IL-5, which are responsible for allergic inflammation, while increasing IL-12 levels. This suggests a potential role for beta-glucans as an adjunct therapy for allergic diseases. Arthritis Beta-glucans have been found to reduce oxidative tissue damage in arthritis, suggesting their potential role in managing arthritic diseases. Additional Functions Beta-glucans from cereals and mushrooms have been shown to lower serum cholesterol and LDL levels, reducing the risk of atherosclerosis and heart disease. They also improve bowel motility and may help alleviate intestinal problems like constipation. In the central nervous system, beta-glucans activate microglial cells, which play a role in conditions like Alzheimer’s disease, AIDS, ischemia injury, and multiple sclerosis. Absorption and Dosage Beta-glucans are best absorbed on an empty stomach. Enterocytes facilitate their transport across the intestinal wall into the lymphatic system, where they interact with macrophages to activate immune function. Both small and large fragments of beta-glucans are absorbed into the serum, as confirmed by radiolabeled studies. The typical dosage of beta-glucans ranges from 40 mg to 3000 mg daily, depending on body weight and whether they are used for maintenance or acute conditions. For maintenance, doses of 40-500 mg per day are common, while acute conditions may require 500-3000 mg per day. Safety and Contraindications Beta-glucans are generally recognized as safe (GRAS) by the FDA. Side effects are rare but may include occasional allergic reactions.
